title: Cc No. 8749/2018 M.L. Joshi vs Suresh Thapa 1 Of 21 on 12 October, 2020
full_text: Cc No. 8749/2018 M.L. Joshi vs Suresh Thapa 1 Of 21 on 12 October, 2020 IN THE COURT IF MS. SHILPI SINGH, METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE-04 NI ACT (SOUTH), SAKET COURT, NEW DELHI CT No. 8749/2018 ML JOSHI V. SURESH THAPA Complaint Case Number 8749/2018 Name and address of the ML Joshi s/o Sh VD Joshi, R/oD- complainant 55, Sector-47, Noida, UP Name and address of the Suresh Thapa s/o Yam Bahadur accused Thapa R/o Quarter No. 310, Type II Delhi Administration Flats, Nimari Colony, Ashok Vihar, Delhi Offence complained of or Under Section 138 of The proved Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 . Plea of the accused Pleaded not guilty. Final Order Acquittal Date of institution 02.07.2018 Date on which reserved 10.09.2020 for Judgment Date of Judgment 12.10.2020 CC NO. 8749/2018 M.L. JOSHI VS.SURESH THAPA 1 of 21 BRIEF STATEMENT OF FACTS FOR THE DECISION 1. Succinctly, it is the case of the complainant that on account of good relations, the accused had taken a friendly loan from the complainant on various occasions, i.e Rs. 50,000/- on 03.08.2012; Rs. 80,000/- on 04.10.2012; Rs. 1,00,000/- on 02.12.2012; Rs. 1,30,000/- on 12.10.2013; Rs. 2,00,000/- on 04.03.2014. That to discharge the legal liability for the total loan amount of Rs. 5,60,000/-, the accused issued two cheque's bearing number, 878032 dated 25.04.18 for a sum of Rs. 3,00,000/- and 878033 dated 27.04.18 for a sum of Rs. 2,60,000/-, both drawn on his bank account maintained with SBI bank at Saket, New Delhi- 17 (hereinafter referred to as the cheques in question) in favour of the complainant. The said cheque's in question were returned unpaid upon presentation on account of 'Funds insufficient' vide return memo dt. 08.05.18. The legal demand notice was duly sent by the complainant to the accused on 24.05.18 but the accused chose not to reply to the same. Since the accused failed to pay the cheque amount within the statutory period, the complainant filed the present complaint u/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act (hereinafter referred to as NI Act ). 2. Upon service of summons, accused entered an appearance in the present matter on 06.09.18 and was admitted to bail. Notice u/s 251 Cr.P.C. was served upon accused on the same date, to which the accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. In his statement of defence, accused stated that the Cheque's in question were issued in a blank signed condition by way of security, to the complainant in the year 2012 for the loan of Rs. 1,00,000/- advanced by the complainant to the accused. He further stated that the said loan was repaid in the year 2013 and hence, he is not liable to pay the alleged cheque amount. He admitted the receipt of legal demand notice and submitted that he did not reply to the CC NO. 8749/2018 M.L. JOSHI VS.SURESH THAPA 2 of 21 same. Thereafter, accused was allowed to cross-examine the complainant u/s 145 (2) NI Act. After cross-examination of the complainant, the matter was fixed for recording statement of the accused u/s 313 Cr.P.C. In the said statement recorded on 04.07.19, the accused stated that he never took any friendly loan of Rs. 5,60,000/- from the complainant but only took a loan of Rs. 1,00,000/- from the complainant which was repaid and the cheques in question were only issued by way of security. Matter was thereafter fixed for leading defence evidence. Despite opportunity, the accused chose not to lead DE and thus, it was closed on 25.11.2019 and the Final arguments were addressed on 24.08.2020. 3. In order to support his case, the complainant stepped into the witness box as CW-1 and rendered his affidavit CW1/1 into evidence where averments made in the complaint were reiterated. He also relied upon various documents such as Ex CW1/A and Ex CW1/B, which are the cheques in question, Ex CW1/C and Ex CW1/D, which are the cheque return memo's dated 08.05.2018, Ex CW1/E is the legal demand notice, sent by the complainant to the accused, demanding the payment and Ex CW1/F and Ex CW1/G are the postal receipts. 4. In his cross examination CW-1 submitted that he met the accused through a common friend in the year 2005 and on 3 rd August 2012, the accused informed him that he was in need of financial assistance for purchasing of property or family functions. As per CW1, the accused used to give similar reason on every date when the loan was advanced to him and on 03.08.2012, the accused gave the cheques in question to him. The complainant could not explain as to why two cheque's were issued by the complainant and he even denied the suggestion that Rs. 50,000/- were advanced on two occasions to the accused which was repaid by him in the year 2013. CW-1 was also confronted with Ex CW1/D1 and CW1/D2 CC NO. 8749/2018 M.L. JOSHI VS.SURESH THAPA 3 of 21 and he admitted these documents and stated that he had indeed advanced loan to one Deepak Lal Kujur and has also settled a case u/s 138 NI act with Kashi Ram Acharya, before the mediation centre. However, CW-1 denied the suggestion that he was into money lending business or that he has misused the cheque's in question. 5. Accused on the other hand did not lead DE, despite opportunity. 6. I have heard the arguments and also gone through the record carefully. 7. It has been vociferously argued by the counsel for the complainant, that the issuance and the signature on the cheques in question are not disputed by the accused and the accused also admits the receipt of legal demand notice, hence presumption under section 118 (a) and 139 of the NI Act are are in favour of the complainant. He further submits that the accused has failed to prove that the cheques in question were handed over in the year 2012 and as the cheques were issued in April 2018, the accused voluntarily acknowledged the liability of the loan received from the complainant. Further, to support the contention that time barred debts are legally enforceable under section 138 NI Act, the complainant has filed the following judgments:  H Narasimha Rao v. Venkataram R; Crl Appeal No. 377/2002, Karnataka High Court, Para 13: "the accused has not disputed his signatures on the dishonoured cheque in question. Therefore, it constitutes an agreement or promise by the debtor to pay the time barred debt. Since the accused has not paid the cheque amount despite the demand made by the complainant, the accused has committed an offence under section 138 of the act. The Learned Magistrate has committed CC NO. 8749/2018 M.L. JOSHI VS.SURESH THAPA 4 of 21 an error in dismissing the complaint and recording an order of acquittal in favour of the accused."  M/s SV Enterprises v. Sri Tulasiram V Friends Cine Creations; 2020 ACD 289, Karnataka High Court, Para 8: "Once the cheque has proved that the same was issued with a reference to any debt, even if it is the time barred debt, in such an eventuality the stand is not available to the accused that there is no existence of any debt or liability. Therefore, on the said ground, the acquittal recorded by the Trial Court is not proper."  Shri Sangameshwar Chits Pvt Ltd v. Sri GR Marigoudar; Crl Appeal No. 2506/2009, Karnataka High Court, Para 7: "therefore, in the present case on hand, notwithstanding that the appellate court has found that the amount due from the respondent was what time barred debt, which could not be recovered by recourse to filing a civil suit for recovery of such money. The cheque issued in discharge of such a debt was not an instrument, cannot be accepted. The logic that nothing prevents a man from repaying a time barred debt, voluntarily, and in the place of legal tender, if the very man issues a cheque in due repayment of such a time barred debt, it is a promise made to discharge such a debt by virtue of issuance of cheque. Therefore, the cheque not being disputed as having been issued by the respondent is a voluntary payment made for a time barred debt. It cannot, therefore be said, that it was not enforceable and if the cheque has been dishonoured for want of sufficiency of funds, it is clearly an offence punishable under section 138 of the NI Act." CC NO. 8749/2018 M.L. JOSHI VS.SURESH THAPA 5 of 21 8. Per contra, the counsel for the accused submits that since the complainant failed to explain the purpose for which the loan was advanced, the fact that the loan was advanced in the year 2012 over a period of 20 months, allegedly for construction of property/ family function and that the demand was only made in April 2018, shows the mala fide of the complainant. The counsel further submits that the complainant failed to explain as to why two cheques were issued for the alleged loan amount, which was already known to the accused, that the complainant had also been advancing friendly loan to other parties and was working as a money lender and that the cheque's were admittedly issued in the year 2018, for a loan advanced in the year 2012, makes the debt time barred and the complaint not maintainable. To buttress his arguments, the counsel for the accused has relied on the following judgments:  Smt Ashwini Satish Bhat v. Shri Jeevan Divakar Lolienkar & Anr , (2000) 5 Bom Cr 9, Bombay High Court, Para 7 & 8; " The ruling upon which reliance has been placed by the learned advocate for the respondent is applicable on all fours. In that case loan was advanced in the year 1985 and the cheque was issued in the year 1990. By the time the cheque was issued, the debt was barred by limitation because no acknowledgement was obtained before the expiry of 3 years from the date of loan. In these circumstances, it was held there that the debt was not legally enforceable at the time of issuance of cheque and the accused could not be punished under section 138 of the said Act. In the light of Explanation to the said section, it was further held therein that in case a cheque is issued for time barred debt and it is dishonoured, the accused cannot be convicted under section 138 on the ground that the said debt was not legally recoverable. CC NO. 8749/2018 M.L. JOSHI VS.SURESH THAPA 6 of 21  Basalingappa v. Mudibassappa , (2019) 5 SCC 418, Para 28: "There is one more aspect of the matter which also needs to be noticed. In the complaint filed by the complainant as well as in examination-in- chief the complainant has not mentioned as to on which date, the loan of Rs 6 lakhs was given to the accused. It was during cross-examination, he gave the date as November 2011. Under Section 118(b) , a presumption shall be made as to date that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn on such date. Admittedly, the cheque is dated 27-2- 2012, there is not even a suggestion by the complainant that a post- dated cheque was given to him in November 2011 bearing the date 27- 2-2012. Giving of a cheque on 27-2-2012, which was deposited on 1-3- 2012 is not compatible with the case of the complainant when we read the complaint submitted by the complainant".  Vijay Polymers Pvt Ltd & Anr v M/s Vinnay Aggarwal, (2009) 162 DLT 23, Delhi High Court, Para 13. In this case, the Bombay High Court decision, in the case of Smt Ashwini Satish Bhat v. Shri Jeevan Divakar Lolienkar & Anr , (2000) 5 Bom Cr 9, was uphel wherein a case under 138 NI Act was not maintainable if the cheque was issued for a time barred debt.  Prajan Kumar Jain v Ravi Malhotra , (2009) 113 DRJ 275, Delhi High Court, Para 14, " In the instant case, the two cheques which are the subject matter of this complaint were for the discharge of a liability of a debt arising out of the agreement dated 14.6.2000 which debt had become time barred. This debt was not a legally enforceable debt within the meaning of Section 138 Explanation of the NI Act. Complaint and all proceedings emanating therefrom are accordingly quashed."  Joseph v Devassia , 2001 Crl LJ 24, Kerela High Court, Para 9, "The learned counsel for the appellant placed strong reliance on the decision of the Madras High Court reported in S. Krishnamurthy v. A.R. CC NO. 8749/2018 M.L. JOSHI VS.SURESH THAPA 7 of 21 Rajan(1996 Crl. Law Journal 3552). In that case, it was contended for the accused that the cheque in question dated 23.4.1989 alleged to have been issued in respect of the debts including under the promissory notes dated 20.3.1985 and 8.4.1985 is not in respect of legally enforceable debts or liabilities, within the meaning of S. 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act since the debts under the pronotes are barred by limitation on the date of issuance of the cheque dated 23.4.1989. But, the court found that in respect of the alleged two time barred pronotes, the accused has paid interest on various dates and thereby the pronotes have not become time barred. In this case, the complainant has no case that the accused has paid interest on the amount borrowed from him in 1987 and there is valid acknowledgement of the debt within the period of limitation. As noticed earlier, since there was no acknowledgement of the debt before the expiry of three years from the date of loan, the debt was not legally enforceable at the time of issuance of the cheque." 9. Now, In order to prove an offence under section 138 NI Act, the following ingredients are required to be fulfilled: i. That there is a legally enforceable debt or liability; ii. That drawer of the cheque issued the cheque to discharge in part or whole of the said legally enforceable debt or liability; iii. The cheque so issued was returned unpaid by the banker of the drawer; iv. Legal demand notice was served upon the accused and the accused failed to make the payment within 15 days of the receipt of the said notice. 10. The object of the statute is to facilitate smooth functioning of business transactions. The provision is necessary as in many transactions cheques are issued merely as a device to defraud the creditors. CC NO. 8749/2018 M.L. JOSHI VS.SURESH THAPA 8 of 21 Dishonour of cheque causes incalculable loss, injury and inconvenience to the payee and credibility of business transactions suffers a setback. Offence under Section 138 of the Act is primarily a civil wrong. Burden of proof is on accused in view of the presumption under Section 139 which says that, "It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque, of the nature referred to in Section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability." but the standard of such proof is "preponderance of probabilities". Also, in a significant departure from the general rule applicable to contracts, Section 118 of the Act provides certain presumptions to be raised. This section lays down some special rules of evidence relating to presumptions. The reason for these presumptions is that, negotiable instrument passes from hand to hand on endorsement and it would make trading very difficult and negotiability of the instrument impossible, unless certain presumptions are made. The presumption, therefore, is a matter of principle to facilitate negotiability as well as trade. 11. Section 118 of the Act, inter alia, directs that it shall be presumed, until the contrary is proved, that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration. Section 139 of the Act stipulates that unless the contrary is proved, it shall be presumed, that the holder of the cheque received the cheque, for the discharge of whole or part of any debt or liability. Applying the definition of the word "proved" in Section 3 of the Evidence Act to the provisions of Sections 118 and 139 of the Act, it becomes evident that in a trial under Section 138 of the Act a presumption will have to be made that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration and that it was executed for discharge of debt or liability once the execution of negotiable instrument is either proved or admitted. As soon as the complainant discharges the burden to prove that the instrument, the rules of presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 of the Act help him shift the burden on the accused. The presumptions will live, exist and survive and shall end only when the contrary is proved by the accused, that is, the cheque was not CC NO. 8749/2018 M.L. JOSHI VS.SURESH THAPA 9 of 21 issued for consideration and in discharge of any debt or liability. A presumption is not in itself evidence, but only makes a prima facie case for a party for whose benefit it exists. 12. In the present case, two main issues are to be decided:  Is the complaint not maintainable as the accused alleges that the complainant is a professional money lender.  No offence u/s 138 NI Act was committed as the alleged debt was time barred. 13. As far the question of existence of basic ingredients for drawing of presumption under Sections 118 and 139 the NI Act is concerned, it is apparent that the accused admitted his signature on the cheques in question that had been drawn in favour of the complainant, on a bank account maintained by the accused. The said cheques were presented to the Bank concerned within the period of their validity and were returned unpaid for the reason funds insufficient. All the basic ingredients of Section 138 are made out and the onus, now shifts on the accused to establish a probable defence to rebut such presumption.. 14. Now the first line of defence adopted by the accused was that the complainant is a professional money lender who has not even disclosed his source of funds and that the cheque's in question were only issued by way of security which were misused by the complainant. The accused, though admits the issuance and signature on the cheque's in question but he stated that the loan advanced by the complainant was of Rs. 1,00,000/- and not Rs. 5,60,000/- and that the cheques's were issued by way of security at the time of advancement of loan in the year 2012. In the cross examination of the complainant, the counsel for the accused had confronted him with Ex CW1/D1 and Ex CW1/D2, which were admitted by the complainant. The said documents were placed on record to prove the fact that the complainant had advanced loan to other people apart the accused, and had filed cases u/s 138 NI Act against them too. CC NO. 8749/2018 M.L. JOSHI VS.SURESH THAPA 10 of 21 The accused basically wanted to prove that the loan was not a friendly loan but a commercial transaction and that the complainant was in the business of money lending. 15. At this stage, it is important to understand Section 2(8) of Punjab Registration of Money-lenders' Act, 1938. Section 2 of the act is the Definitions clause- "In this Act, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context"- Section 2(8) : "Loan" means an advance whether secured or unsecured of money or in kind at interest and shall include any transaction which the court finds to be in substance a loan, but it shall not include - (i) an advance in kind made by a landlord to his tenant for the purposes of husbandry; Provided the market value of the return does not exceed the market value of the advance as estimated at the time of advance. (ii) a deposit of money or other property in a Government Post Office Bank, or any other Bank, or with a company, or with a co-operative society or with any employer as security from his employees; (iii) a loan to, or by, or a deposit with any society or association registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860 , or under any other enactment; (iv) a loan advanced by or to the Central or any State Government or by or to any local body under the authority of the Central or any State Government; (v) a loan advanced by a bank, a co-operative Society or a company whose accounts are subject to audit by a certificated auditor under the Indian Companies Act, 1913 ; (vi) a loan advanced by a trader to a trader, in the regular course of business, in accordance with trade usage; (vii) an advance made on the basis of a negotiable instrument as defined in the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 , other than a promissory note. CC NO. 8749/2018 M.L. JOSHI VS.SURESH THAPA 11 of 21 16. A bare reading of Section 2(8)(vii) states that, loan does not include a loan advanced on the basis of a negotiable instrument as defined in the negotiable instruments act, 1881. Therefore, if a person, even though he is a money lender without a license, advances a loan to someone on the basis of a cheque, then it cannot be said that the case is barred as per Punjab Registration of Money lender's Act. Rather, these kind of cases are expressly exempted from the act and the complainant, even if an unregistered money lender, files a case to recover the money on the basis of a cheque issued by the accused, then the case is valid and maintainable. Further, Section 138 of the act was enacted with the object to improve the credibility of transactions by the negotiable instruments and to facilitate the bank transaction in a smooth manner. It is experienced that recourse to criminal trial is preferred than a civil suit, as it does not requires Court fees and is quicker. However, the section is penal with severe consequences and therefore the section warrants a strict construction on the proof of the facts. If all the ingredients under section 138 NI Act are proved by the complainant then presumption under section 139 of the act stand in his favour and the complaint, even if filed by an unregistered moneylender, is perfectly maintainable. Hence, considering the above discussion, the defence of the accused that the complainant is a money lender and therefore, the case is not maintainable, holds no water. 17. The next defence of the accused was that the cheque's in question were issued in the year 2012 for the loan of Rs. 1,00,000/- advanced by the complainant and that the said loan was repaid in the year 2013. It is the case of the accused that the loan amount that was borrowed from the complainant, was already repaid in the year 2013 and that the case is otherwise also not maintainable as it is filed for recovery of a time barred debt. At this juncture, it would be appropriate and necessary to first reproduce the provisions of Section 138 of the NI Act, which read as under: CC NO. 8749/2018 M.L. JOSHI VS.SURESH THAPA 12 of 21 "138. Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the account: Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for [a term which may be extended to two years], or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both: Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless-- (a) the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; (b) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, [within thirty days] of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid; and (c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice. Explanation. -- For the purposes of this section, "debt or other liability" means a legally enforceable debt or other liability." CC NO. 8749/2018 M.L. JOSHI VS.SURESH THAPA 13 of 21 18. It would also be appropriate to take note of Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 which deals with the effect of acknowledgement which reads as under:-- "18. Effect of acknowledgment in writing: (1) Where, before the expiration of the prescribed period for a suit of application in respect of any property or right, an acknowledgment of liability in respect of such property or right has been made in writing signed by the party against whom such property or right is claimed, or by any person through whom he derives his title or liability, a fresh period of limitation shall be computed from the time when the acknowledgment was so signed. (2) Where the writing containing the acknowledgment is undated, oral evidence may be given of the time when it was signed; but subject to the provisions of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (1 of 1872), oral evidence of its contents shall not be received. Explanation.--For the purposes of this section,-- (a) an acknowledgment may be sufficient though it omits to specify the exact nature of the property or right, or avers that the time for payment, delivery, performance or enjoyment has not yet come or is accompanied by a refusal to pay, deliver, perform or permit to enjoy, or is coupled with a claim to set off, or is addressed to a person other than a person entitled to the property or right, CC NO. 8749/2018 M.L. JOSHI VS.SURESH THAPA 14 of 21 (b) the word "signed" means signed either personally or by an agent duly authorised in this behalf, and (c) an application for the execution of a decree or order shall not be deemed to be an application in respect of any property or right." 19. Perusal of the aforesaid provisions clearly goes on to show that for analyzing the limitation of a liability beyond a period of three years, the acknowledgment, if any, must be made before the period of limitation is over. The counsel for the complainant has relied on various judgments of Karnataka High Court (supra), wherein it was held that a cheque, even if issued for the repayment of a time barred debt, gets dishonoured, then a case under section 138 NI Act is maintainable and the accused will be said to have committed the offence under the said Act. 20. Before the evidence adduced by both the parties are assessed qua the time barred debt and if it is legally recoverable or not, reference may be made to the case titled, Sasseriyil Joseph v. Devassia , 2001 Cri LJ 24, Kerela High Court, para 10, "In this case, the complainant has no case that the accused has paid interest on the amount borrowed from him in 1987 and there is valid acknowledgement of the debt within the period of limitation. As noticed earlier, since there was no acknowledgement of the debt before the expiry of three years from the date of loan, the debt was not legally enforceable at the time of issuance of the cheque." This Judgment was further appealed by the complainant and a SLP was filed before the Apex Court. The Apex Court, V.O.D 10.09.2001, in SLP (Crl) No. 1785 of 2001 held that, "We have heard learned counsel for the petitioner. We have perused the judgment of the High Court of Kerala in Criminal Appeal No. 161 of 1994 confirming the CC NO. 8749/2018 M.L. JOSHI VS.SURESH THAPA 15 of 21 judgment/order of acquittal passed by the Addl. Sessions Judge, Thalassery in Criminal Appeal No. 212 of 1992 holding inter alia that the cheque in question having been issued by the accused for due which was barred by limitation the penal provision under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act is not attracted in the case. On the facts of the case as available on the records and the clear and unambiguous provision in the explanation to Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act the judgment of the lower appellate Court as confirmed by the High Court is unassailed. Therefore, the special leave petition is dismissed." 21. Thus, the Apex Court upheld the decision of the Kerela High Court and stated that the penal provision under section 138 NI Act is not attracted for a time barred debt. The important point to note in this order was that it was based on the facts of the case as available on the record. Later, another judgment was passed by the Apex Court, A.V. Murthy v. B.S. Nagabasavanna , (2002) 2 SCC 642, wherein the summons issued by the Magistrate against the accused were quashed by the first Appellate Court, on the ground that the the case of the complainant was based for the recovery of a time barred debt. The decision of the first appellate court was upheld by the Karnataka High Court and thereafter the appeal was preferred to the Hon'ble Supreme court. The Apex Court held in Para 5 and 6, " As the complaint has been rejected at the threshold, we do not propose to express any opinion on this question as the matter is yet to be agitated by the parties. But, we are of the view that the learned Sessions Judge and the learned Single Judge of the High Court were clearly in error in quashing the complaint proceedings. Under Section 118 of the Act, there is a presumption that until the contrary is proved, every negotiable instrument was drawn for consideration. Even under Section 139 of the Act, it is specifically stated that it shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder CC NO. 8749/2018 M.L. JOSHI VS.SURESH THAPA 16 of 21 of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in Section 138 for discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. It is also pertinent to note that under sub-section (3) of Section 25 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a promise, made in writing and signed by the person to be charged therewith, or by his agent generally or specially authorized in that behalf, to pay wholly or in part a debt of which the creditor might have enforced payment but for the law for the limitation of suits, is a valid contract. Moreover, in the instant case, the appellant has submitted before us that the respondent, in his balance sheet prepared for every year subsequent to the loan advanced by the appellant, had shown the amount as deposits from friends. A copy of the balance sheet as on 31-3- 1997 is also produced before us. If the amount borrowed by the respondent is shown in the balance sheet, it may amount to acknowledgment and the creditor might have a fresh period of limitation from the date on which the acknowledgment was made. However, we do not express any final opinion on all these aspects, as these are matters to be agitated before the Magistrate by way of defence of the respondent. This is not a case where the cheque was drawn in respect of a debt or liability, which was completely barred from being enforced under law. If for example, the cheque was drawn in respect of a debt or liability payable under a wagering contract, it could have been said that that debt or liability is not legally enforceable as it is a claim, which is prohibited under law. This case is not a case of that type. But we are certain that at this stage of the proceedings, to say that the cheque drawn by the respondent was in respect of a debt or liability, which was not legally enforceable, was clearly illegal and erroneous." 22. It was on the basis of this judgment that Karnataka High Court held in H Narasimha Rao v. Venkataram R ; Crl Appeal No. 377/2002 and M/s SV Enterprises v. Sri Tulasiram V Friends Cine CC NO. 8749/2018 M.L. JOSHI VS.SURESH THAPA 17 of 21 Creations; 2020 ACD 289, that the penal provision of section 138 NI is attracted even if the case is based on recovery of a time barred debt. However, the decision of the Apex court in A.V. Murthy v. B.S. Nagabasavanna , (2002) 2 SCC 642 was based on the fact that the accused had reflected in his balance sheet the friendly loan taken from the complainant. The said amount was reflected within the period of 3 years and would amount to acknowledgment as per Section 18 of the Limitation Act. The Apex Court had set aside the quashing of summoning order as the factum of acknowledgment of debt was ignored during the quashment and the said fact was matter of Trial. The Apex Court had nowhere in this judgment held that a case under section 138 NI Act is maintainable even for a time barred debt. This was not the question before the Hon'ble Supreme Court and neither was it decided in this case. Rather, considering these facts, the order of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Sasseriyil Joseph v. Devassia (supra) had upheld that time barred debts are not recoverable even if a cheque is issued and a case under section 138 NI Act is filed, if the debt was not acknowledged within the period of limitation. 23. In fact, this principle was reiterated by the Hon'ble Delhi High Court in Jage Ram Karan Singh and Another v. State and Another , 2019 SCC OnLine Del 9486, Para 33, "Therefore, I do not agree with the contention raised by the learned counsel for the petitioners that the Appellate Court has misinterpreted Section 139 of the NI Act. The Appellate Court has rightly held that the alleged responsibility of the respondent No. 2, if any, had already become time-barred as on the date of the issuance of cheque and, therefore, the same cannot be said to be in discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability. The judgments relied upon by the petitioners are of no help in view of the legal position and the law discussed herein-above." CC NO. 8749/2018 M.L. JOSHI VS.SURESH THAPA 18 of 21 24. Coming back to the facts of this case, the complainant has admittedly stated in his complaint and in cross examination that the loan was advanced from 2012 to 2014. The last date on which the loan was advanced was 04.03.2014. Though, in his cross examination, the complainant has stated that the cheques were issued in the year 2012 but later it was submitted by the counsel for the complainant in the oral as well as written arguments that the cheques were issued in the year 2018 which is in itself acknowledgement of the time barred debt. The complainant has also stated in his complaint as well as evidence by way of affidavit that the cheque's in question were issued in the year 2018. Now if the period of limitation is calculated, the cause of action to enforce the said liability, as per law, against the accused remained in existence for the loan advanced in 2012 only till 2015 and for the loan advanced in 2014, it expired on 04.03.2017. Nowhere has the complainant stated in his complaint or his evidence that the alleged loans were acknowledged by the accused within the period of limitation. The complainant has also not placed any document on record to show that the period of limitation was extended. In fact, it was never the case of the complainant that the period of limitation was extended and from day one, he was claiming a time barred debt. The only argument addressed on behalf of the complainant was that once a cheque is issued, even if it is for a time barred debt, then the case under section 138 NI Act is maintainable. 25. The said proposition has already been decided by the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi in Vijay Polymers Pvt Ltd & Anr v M/s Vinnay Aggarwal, (2009) 162 DLT 23, Prajan Kumar Jain v Ravi Malhotra, (2009) 113 DRJ 275 and Jage Ram Karan Singh and Another v. State and Another, 2019 SCC OnLine Del 9486. These cases were based on similar facts and the law in this regard is already settled. CC NO. 8749/2018 M.L. JOSHI VS.SURESH THAPA 19 of 21 Moreover, the cheque's in question relied upon by the complainant were also issued after the expiry of period of limitation, therefore, the complainant cannot bring the issue of liability within the time frame. Though, it is correct that once the signatures are admitted on the cheque, existence of legally enforceable debt or liability has to be presumed, but it is to be noted that the said presumption is rebuttable and in the instant matter, the accused has been able to rebut the said presumption by showing that the liability for payment arose in 2015, 2016 and 2017 and since the case was filed in the year 2018, Limitation had already expired by then. Also, the defence taken by the accused was that the loan was repaid in the year 2013 and the cheque's in question were security cheque's. To show that the cheque's were misused, the accused had put forth the defence of a time barred debt. 26. Further, it is also well-settled that the presumption, which is contained in Section 139 of the NI Act, only raises the presumption that the cheque has been issued for the discharge of a debt or liability and existence of legally recoverable debt is not a matter of presumption, as per the aforesaid provisions of law. Mere issuance of a cheque, without anything more, cannot revive a time-barred debt, because cheque has to be given, as contemplated by the explanatory, in discharge of a legally enforceable debt. In the present case, the accused has put forth a probable defence and through the admissions of the complainant has brought on record that the debt which the complainant is trying to recover has already become time barred and the presumption under section 139 NI Act cannot be said to be in his favour as the presumption is only for a legally recoverable debt, which is not the scenario in this case. CC NO. 8749/2018 M.L. JOSHI VS.SURESH THAPA 20 of 21 27. Thus, in view of the above discussion and considering the settled position of Law in this case, this court is of the opinion that the presumption under section 139 NI act is not in favour of the complainant as the alleged loan was a time barred debt and no evidence is placed on record to show that the debt was acknowledged by the accused within the period of limitation. The accused though, has not stepped in the witness box but he has adduced cogent evidence at the stage of cross examination and conclusively established the fact that the alleged debt was time barred. Since the debt in the present case is not legally recoverable, this Court finds the accused not guilty of the offence under section 138 of NI Act and acquits the accused Suresh Thapa from this case. 28. The accused is directed to furnish bail bond and surety bond in the sum of Rs. 50,000 u/s 437 (A) CrPC and is directed to be present before the Ld. Appellate Court as and when notice is served upon him. Bail Bonds are not furnished. Put up for filing of bail bonds on 19.10.2020.
